Understanding
Makefiles
Automating builds with make —targets,
dependencies, and reproducible workflows
What Is a Makefile?
▪A Makefile is a plain-text file that tells the make tool how to build a
project.
▪It describes what to build, what each output depends on, and the
exact commands that produce it.
▪Running make reads these rules and executes only the steps
needed to bring outputs up to date.
THE IDEA
make + Makefile = a small,
declarative build system.
You declare the goals and dependencies; make
figures out the order and the work.
Why Use Make?
1
Incremental builds
Rebuilds only what actually
changed by comparing file
timestamps — a big time-saver
on large projects.
2
Dependency tracking
Understands how files relate,
so nothing is skipped and
nothing is built out of order.
3
Reproducible
One command runs the whole
pipeline the same way, every
time, on any machine.
4
Language-agnostic
Drives C, LaTeX, data pipelines,
or deployments — anything
expressed as commands.
Anatomy of a Rule
Every rule in a Makefile follows the same three-part shape:
target: prerequisites
recipe
Target
The file to create — or a name to run.
Prerequisites
The inputs the target depends on.
Recipe
Shell commands, each indented with a real TAB.
The TAB before each recipe line is required — spaces will not work.
A Simple Example
A tiny Makefile that compiles and links a C program:
hello: main.o utils.o
cc -o hello main.o utils.o
main.o: main.c
cc -c main.c
utils.o: utils.c
cc -c utils.c
$ make hello
make checks timestamps and rebuilds
only the .o files that are out of date, then
links them into hello.
Change one .c file and re-run — only that
object is recompiled.
Variables & Automatic Variables
Your own variables
CC = gcc
CFLAGS = -Wall -O2
Define compilers, flags, and paths once, then reuse them
everywhere with $(CC) and $(CFLAGS). Change a setting in a single
place.
Automatic variables
$@ the target name
$< the first prerequisite
$^ all prerequisites
%.o: %.c
$(CC) $(CFLAGS) -c $< -o $@
Phony Targets & Pattern Rules
Phony targets
.PHONY: clean all
clean:
rm -f *.o hello
Names that are actions, not files. Marking them .PHONY means
they always run — even if a file called clean exists.
Pattern rules
%.o: %.c
$(CC) $(CFLAGS) -c $< -o $@
One rule builds any .o from its matching .c. No need to write a
separate rule per file — make fills in the blanks.
Best Practices & Takeaways
Keep it DRY
Use variables for compilers and flags, and pattern rules to avoid repeating yourself.
Declare .PHONY targets
Mark non-file actions like clean, all, test, and install so they always run.
Indent with real TABs
Recipe lines must start with a TAB — spaces cause hard-to-spot errors.
Make it discoverable
Put an all target first as the default, and add a help target.
Make turns a set of dependencies into a fast, repeatable build.
A Complete Example: The Code
Three source files that make will compile and link into one program.
/* greet.h */
#ifndef GREET_H
#define GREET_H
void greet(const char *name);
#endif
/* greet.c */
#include <stdio.h>
#include "greet.h"
void greet(const char *name) {
printf("Hello, %s!\n", name);
}
/* main.c */
#include "greet.h"
int main(void) {
greet("Make");
return 0;
}
The Makefile, Build & Run
Type make to build, run ./hello, then make clean to remove the build outputs.
Makefile
CC = gcc
CFLAGS = -Wall -O2
hello: main.o greet.o
$(CC) $(CFLAGS) -o hello main.o greet.o
main.o: main.c greet.h
$(CC) $(CFLAGS) -c main.c
greet.o: greet.c greet.h
$(CC) $(CFLAGS) -c greet.c
.PHONY: clean
clean:
rm -f hello *.o
Terminal
$ make
# make compiles main.c and greet.c, then links them into
hello — automatically.
$ ./hello
Hello, Make!
# run the built program to see its output.
$ make clean
# clean deletes hello and the .o files for a fresh
rebuild.
Summary
The essentials of make, at a glance.
What make does
Reads a Makefile's rules and rebuilds only what is out of date, by
comparing file timestamps.
Anatomy of a rule
A target, its prerequisites, then a TAB-indented recipe of shell
commands.
Stay DRY
Define variables once; use pattern rules and automatic
variables to avoid repetition.
Build & run
Type make to build; .PHONY targets like clean always run, then
run your program.
One Makefile, one command — a fast, reproducible build every time.
